summary: Defines using a MIME multipart/related structure to bundle an HTML page with the images and other resources it references, and a Content-Location header that lets links point to other parts of the same bundle. It obsoletes RFC 2110.

eli5.summary: A web page has pictures that normally come separately. This puts the page and all its pictures in one email package, with labels so links find the right piece.

questions: send html page with images in email
subtitle: How to pack an HTML page and all its pictures into one MIME email, and how links find the right piece.

tldr.problem: An HTML page normally pulls in its images and other resources one by one from URIs, which fails for people who only have email or cannot reach the sender's servers.
tldr.mechanism: The page and every resource it references are bundled in one MIME multipart/related message, and a new Content-Location header labels each part with a URI so links in the page can be matched to parts of the same bundle.
tldr.outcome: A complete multi-resource HTML document travels or is archived as a single message. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2110 and drops its Content-Base header.

today: RFC 2557 is listed as a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no later RFC obsoleting or updating it. It obsoletes RFC 2110, so it is the version of the MHTML specification to read.

sections.title: Aggregate Documents in One Message
sections.content:
An HTML page is a root resource plus subsidiary resources (images, video clips, applets, style sheets) that it references by URI. A browser fetches each one separately, at the moment it displays the page. That does not help when someone wants to send the whole page in one e-mail message.

RFC 2557 solves this in two steps. It uses a MIME multipart/related structure to aggregate the text/html root and the resources it references, and it defines a new MIME header, Content-Location, that lets URIs in the root point at other body parts of the same structure.

The RFC says the same conventions can also be used for resources retrieved by HTTP or FTP, and for storing complete web pages as they looked at one moment. Implementations only have to handle documents whose root is HTML, even though other URI-linked formats such as XML, PDF and VRML are mentioned.
sections.eli5: Imagine mailing a photo book. Instead of sending the text and telling your friend to fetch each photo, you put the text and every photo into one envelope.

sections.title: The Content-Location Header
sections.content:
Content-Location can appear in any message or content heading. Its value is one URI, absolute or relative, that labels the body part it sits on. The ABNF is content-location = "Content-Location:" [CFWS] URI [CFWS], and the URI is limited to the URL syntax of the time.

The URI does not have to be retrievable by everyone. It can point inside a company network or even be fictitious, though an absolute URI SHOULD still be globally unique. A part may carry one Content-Location, alongside its Content-ID and, for messages, a Message-ID. All of these are equally valid labels. Several Content-Location fields in one heading are not allowed.

The URI of an aggregate is not the URI of its root. If a multipart/related heading has a Content-Location, it SHOULD apply to the whole aggregate, not just the root part.

URIs with characters that cannot appear in a header (spaces, for example) MUST be encoded with the MIME part 3 methods, only in the header and never in the HTML text. Receivers MUST decode them before comparing. Long values may be folded, but encoding comes before folding.
sections.eli5: Each item in the envelope gets a sticker with an address on it. The sticker does not need to be a real address that works anywhere, it just needs to be a name the page can use to find that item.

sections.title: Finding the Base URI
sections.content:
A relative URI such as images/logo.gif only means something relative to a base. RFC 2557 gives an ordered list, and the first method that applies wins.

  • A base inside the body part itself, such as the HTML BASE element.
  • An absolute Content-Location in the immediately surrounding heading.
  • The same check, repeated outward through enclosing multipart or message headings.
  • If the MIME object came in an HTTP response, the URI used for the request.
  • Otherwise the base thismessage:/ MUST be used.

The thismessage:/ base exists only to resolve relative references inside a multipart/related structure when nothing else gives a base. It lets a page with a plain reference like ietflogo.gif still match a part labeled Content-Location: ietflogo.gif.
sections.eli5: If a note says "the red door", you need to know which house. The rules say where to look first for the house, and if nothing says, you assume it is this very envelope.

sections.title: Matching Links to Body Parts
sections.content:
For each URI in a text/html body part, the receiver first unfolds header values and removes MIME encodings, without decoding URL percent escapes (the RFC's example: a%2eb/c%20d must not become a/b/c d). It then resolves relative URIs using the base rules above.

Next it compares the resulting string, octet by octet, with the URI derived from the Content-ID and Content-Location headers of other parts in the same or a surrounding multipart/related. Identical strings mean the link refers to that part. A fictitious thismessage:/ URI can only match another such URI. If nothing matches, the receiver may try to fetch the resource over the normal Internet.

Links using the cid: scheme are matched only against Content-ID values. A Content-Location that merely looks like CID: foo@bar.net is ignored. Content-IDs MUST be globally unique, not just unique within a message.

References between parallel or nested multipart/related structures are only partly covered: a nested part may reference parts of the structure enclosing it, but not the other way round, and not between siblings.
sections.eli5: When the page says "show picture X", the reader looks through the envelope for a picture with exactly that label. The label has to match letter for letter.

sections.title: Using multipart/related
sections.content:
When a message holds parts that contain URIs and also holds the resources those URIs name, the whole set SHOULD be sent in a multipart/related structure as defined in RFC 2389. If the start part is a plain object such as text/html, it SHOULD be the root. If the start part is multipart/alternative, an HTML alternative inside it SHOULD be the root. The RFC warns that some receivers treat multipart/alternative as multipart/mixed.

The type parameter is mandatory in the Content-Type header, and when the start part is not first, its Content-ID goes in a start parameter. Within one structure each part MUST have a different Content-ID and a Content-Location that resolves to a different URI.

The RFC lists why bundling helps: recipients who only have e-mail, recipients behind firewalls or with company-internal links, preserving a document even if the linked resources later change or disappear, resources that cannot be fetched by protocol, and faster access. A sender that took objects from the web SHOULD keep their original URIs rather than rewriting them, so message integrity codes still verify. A plain HTML page with no linked parts MAY be sent alone without a multipart/related wrapper.

HTML text in a message must use a declared charset (the RFC says SHOULD include it rather than rely on defaults), and line breaks in text types must be CRLF in MIME, unlike what HTTP allows. A checksum that this breaks SHOULD be removed.
sections.eli5: The envelope has a main page and helpers. The rules say which one is the main page, and that no two helpers may have the same label.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A sender can lie about where a part came from by giving it a Content-Location that names another resource. Receivers should treat that header only as a label for resolving links inside the same structure, not as proof of the resource's source, unless verified another way.

Other risks the RFC lists: URIs, especially file URIs, can leak information from inside a security context; hidden passwords or tickets inside a forwarded page can be exposed; HTML can carry or reference executable content such as JavaScript, so a receiving agent running it without restrictions is called exceedingly dangerous; and a link to an object not included in the message can reveal who is reading it when the object is requested over HTTP.

For caching, a link inside a multipart/related structure SHALL be satisfied by a part of the same structure and not by any other source. A sender who wants the live resource MUST NOT include a labeled copy. A resource received this way MUST NOT be served from a cache except through a reference from the same structure, otherwise the message could inject bogus resources into a shared Web cache.
sections.eli5: A sneaky sender could stick a fake label on something. So the reader should only trust labels for finding things inside the envelope, and should not let envelope contents sneak into the shared library.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2110
sections.content:
RFC 2557 replaces RFC 2110. The text lists these differences:

  • The formats now apply to multipart MIME carried by HTTP or FTP, not just e-mail.
  • A Content-Location in an outer multipart heading can serve as a base for relative URIs in its parts, but only if no base can be derived from the part itself, and a base in an inner heading wins over an outer one.
  • The Content-Base header is removed. An implementer MAY accept it in input for compatibility but MUST never send it.
  • Section 4.4.1 was added to cover URIs with characters that do not fit the header syntax.
  • Relative and absolute matching were merged by treating otherwise unresolvable relative URIs as if they had the base thismessage:/.
sections.eli5: This is the second edition. It got rid of one old label type and added a rule for the case where nothing says which house the address is in.
